tier_reason: The repo README has no numbers and no benchmark code; the only figures come from search snippets of blocked peer-reviewed papers (arXiv 2205.12217, ACM MMSys 2023, and an independent J. Real-Time Image Processing 2023 study), and snippet-only numbers cap the entry at C.

corrections.claimed_speedup: Snippet only (all papers blocked): the arXiv 2205.12217 abstract says OpenVVC reaches real-time UHD decoding by combining SIMD with frame-level parallelism, decodes faster than VVdeC, and uses less memory than VVdeC by a factor greater than 2.11x. An independent study (Journal of Real-Time Image Processing 2023, 'Performance analysis of optimized versatile video coding software decoders on embedded platforms') found OpenVVC and VVdeC both reach real-time FHD on an 8-core and HD on a 4-core embedded platform with comparable energy (about 26 J and 15 J), with VVdeC needing 2x OpenVVC's memory; that is a memory win, not a speed win. The ACM MMSys 2023 end-to-end pipeline (uvg266 encoder + uvgRTP + OpenVVC) is almost 34,000x as fast as a VTM-based pipeline and 3.3x the fastest VVenC/VVdeC configuration; those are whole-pipeline figures that include the encoder, not decoder-only speedups. The 290 fps FHD / 90 fps UHD figures in the original record did not appear in any snippet this verifier saw.
corrections.caveats: Snippet only: every number comes from search snippets of blocked papers (arXiv 2205.12217; ACM MMSys 2023 'Open-Source Toolkit for Live End-to-End 4K VVC Intra Coding'; Springer JRTIP 2023 independent study at https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s11554-023-01376-7); none was opened, and the repo README has no numbers or benchmark harness. The baselines are the VTM reference decoder and Fraunhofer VVdeC, not FFmpeg; no comparison against FFmpeg's native VVC decoder was found. The independent study shows parity in speed with VVdeC and a 2x memory advantage, so the speed claim rests on the authors' own paper. The 34,000x figure is an end-to-end pipeline result dominated by the encoder choice. Last commit on master is 2022-03-22 (2,197 commits), so the code may lag the papers' decoder; README still says 'still under development' and supports only 8-bit bitstreams. LGPL-2.1.

notes: Tier and verdict unchanged; claimed_speedup rewritten to what the snippets support, with the memory-vs-speed distinction and the pipeline nature of the 34,000x figure made explicit. pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov (PiSDF paper) and archive.fosdem.org (FFVVC slides) were tried and are EGRESS_BLOCKED; a paper-access retier could check the arXiv PDF for the 290/90 fps figures and hardware.

tier_reason: First-party README tables against libopus 1.6.1 on a named CPU (Ryzen 7 5700X; Apple M-series model unstated), but the C-comparison benchmark (opus_vs_c_bench) is not public: benches/ holds only opus_bench.rs, which has no libopus arm, and the libopus 1.6.1 source tree and tests/*.c are gitignored. Not A without public comparison code and C build flags.

corrections.claimed_speedup: README tables vs libopus 1.6.1, mono, wall-clock for the full frame set. Ryzen 7 5700X: 8 kHz/20 ms VoIP 39.9 vs 40.6 ms (Rust 2% faster); 16 kHz/20 ms VoIP 66.8 vs 67.1 ms (0.5%); 16 kHz/10 ms VoIP 73.2 vs 72.5 ms (C ahead, within noise); 48 kHz/20 ms Audio 25.1 vs 28.4 ms (12%); 48 kHz/10 ms Audio 29.7 vs 31.2 ms (5%). Apple Silicon M-series (run 2026-04-23): 8 kHz/20 ms 31.47 vs 31.20 ms (C 0.9% faster); 16 kHz/20 ms 51.19 vs 52.81 ms (Rust 3.1%); 16 kHz/10 ms 55.69 vs 55.49 ms (within noise); 48 kHz/20 ms 13.97 vs 19.39 ms (28%); 48 kHz/10 ms 16.19 vs 20.28 ms (20%). The VoIP (SILK) rows are at parity; the gains are in the 48 kHz Audio-application rows.
corrections.compiler_and_flags: README: cargo --release with 'opt-level=3 + ThinLTO'; Cargo.toml has no [profile.release] section (a local .cargo config is gitignored), rustc version not stated; libopus 1.6.1 built from a local opus-1.6.1/ tree that .gitignore excludes, its build flags not stated
corrections.stars_or_usage: 50 stars, 7 forks; crates.io opus-rs 0.1.34: 181,963 downloads (131,859 recent); forked as Remade-With-Rust/rusty-opus
corrections.caveats: Rust crate (language-filter mismatch for a C++-first catalog). The README tells readers to run `cargo bench --bench opus_vs_c_bench`, but no such target exists: benches/ holds only opus_bench.rs (no libopus arm; the opus 0.3 dev-dependency is not used there), Cargo.toml registers only opus_bench, bench_quick.sh filters for 'opus_vs_c_real', and the published 0.1.17 crate (whose date matches the Apple run) has no C bench either; .gitignore excludes opus-1.6.1/ and tests/*.c, so the C comparison cannot be reproduced. The checked-in Rust-only opus_real group does encode plus decode at complexity 0, CBR, 20/64 kbps, with 48 kHz input made by repeating each 16 kHz sample three times, which differs from the README's 'encode-only' description; whether the private C bench matched these settings is unknown. Single speech clip, mono; stereo and music untested. VoIP rows are within noise or favour C. The Apple numbers date from 2026-04-23 (0.1.17) and the CELT encoder was reworked for byte-exactness in August 2026, so the tables may be stale. Tier would be A if the C-comparison benchmark and the libopus build flags were public.

notes: Numbers match the README exactly (the record omitted the 16 kHz/20 ms rows, now added). Confirmed the missing C bench: benches/opus_vs_c_bench.rs and benches/opus_vs_c_real.rs return 404, and the C sources are gitignored. language already reads Rust; verify.py apply ignores the language key, so it is set here only for the record. Lead: Remade-With-Rust/rusty-opus, a fork with AVX2 SILK kernels, claims 1.50x libopus on CELT speech per core (seen in the remade_ffmpeg_rs README); it would need its own record or a duplicate decision.

tier_reason: First-party numbers with public harnesses (tools/bench/codec-bench.ps1, tools/bench/pinab.py, tools/quality/aac_vs_ffmpeg.py) and a pinned toolchain (Rust 1.95.0, thin LTO, codegen-units 1), but no CPU model for the MP3 and AAC rows (docs/benchmarks.md gives only a '24-core box' for Vorbis), no FFmpeg build flags, and no stated command for the MP3 decode table, so not A.

corrections.claimed_speedup: Per component, all first-party. MP3 decode (crate rusty_mp3, crates/rusty_mp3/README.md) vs the FFmpeg CLI's native libavcodec MP3 decoder (`-f null -`, not libmp3lame or mpg123), 27.5-minute stream, decode-and-discard, wall clock, 15 alternated pairs: 1 physical core 1,952 vs 2,431 ms (1.24x, 15/15, z = -3.87); 2 physical cores, pipelined build 1,017 vs 1,455 ms (1.39x); total CPU on one core 1,875 vs 2,125 ms (1.13x less CPU, derived from page data). The same table's control row shows the serial rusty_mp3 build on 2 cores at 1,807 ms against FFmpeg's 1,445 ms, i.e. FFmpeg 1.25x faster (derived from page data), because FFmpeg's CLI spreads work over about 2 cores even with -threads 1. AAC-LC encode (crate rusty_aac) vs FFmpeg 8.1.2's native AAC encoder (`-c:a aac`, not libfdk_aac): main README about 6x faster on a 60 s stereo clip (about 450x realtime) via frame-parallel encoding against FFmpeg's single-threaded encoder, about 1.15x single-thread; the crate README reports 3.2-7.9x (mean 5.0x) on 24 s clips (piano 214x vs 57x realtime, guitar 306x vs 39x, vocal 299x vs 93x), best-of-5, unpinned subprocesses. Vorbis encode (crate rusty_vorbis) vs libvorbis via `ffmpeg -c:a libvorbis`: at about 140 kb/s, 443x realtime on 24 cores vs libvorbis 86x (about 5.2x in docs/benchmarks.md, 5.3x in the README), but single-thread 60x vs 87x realtime (about 1.45x slower than libvorbis), and libvorbis is 0.6-0.7 PEAQ ODG ahead on tonal content at matched bitrate. Image rows (PNG decode 2.55-2.89x, lossy WebP decode 1.24-1.29x vs FFmpeg) are outside video-audio.
corrections.compiler_and_flags: Rust 1.95.0 pinned in rust-toolchain.toml; workspace [profile.release] lto = "thin", codegen-units = 1, panic = "unwind"; default build has no target-cpu flag (AVX kernels are runtime-dispatched); binaries use the in-house rusty_alloc global allocator. FFmpeg 8.1.2 (system build, flags not stated) for the AAC comparison; FFmpeg version for the MP3 and Vorbis rows not stated.
corrections.hardware: Not stated for the MP3 and AAC rows; docs/benchmarks.md names an Intel Core i7-14650HX for VP9 decode and only a '24-core box' for the Vorbis rows; the harnesses are Windows PowerShell/psutil scripts pinning to one core at High priority
corrections.stars_or_usage: 6 stars, 0 forks; crates.io rusty_mp3 0.8.0 (42,200 downloads), rusty_aac 0.5.0 (7,824), rusty_vorbis 0.1.1 (1,668), all pointing to this repo; README claims 175,858 active installs through MATA Disco (not verifiable)
corrections.caveats: Rust workspace (language-filter mismatch for a C++-first catalog); one repo holds several crates and each number belongs to one of them: MP3 decode to rusty_mp3, AAC encode to rusty_aac, Vorbis encode to rusty_vorbis; any standalone listing needs a paper: id. The only per-core speed win of substance is MP3 decode (1.24x on one physical core, about 1.13x less CPU, derived), measured against the FFmpeg CLI rather than libavcodec directly, and the README's own control row has FFmpeg 1.25x ahead of the serial rusty_mp3 build on two cores; the 1.39x two-core figure uses a two-thread pipeline. AAC's 5-6x and Vorbis's 5.3x are multi-threaded frame-parallel encodes against single-threaded encoders (different work); single-thread AAC is about 1.15x faster and single-thread Vorbis is about 1.45x slower than libvorbis, with lower PEAQ quality at matched bitrate. docs/benchmarks.md lists MP3 and AAC decode as 'not yet benchmarked' even though the READMEs carry MP3 decode numbers. Harness code is public (tools/bench/codec-bench.ps1, tools/bench/pinab.py, tools/quality/aac_vs_ffmpeg.py) but the CPU model and FFmpeg build flags for the audio rows are not stated. The earlier CLI-to-CLI comparison had MP3 decode 1.20x behind before output and profiling asymmetries were removed. Video rows are slower than FFmpeg (VP9 decode 0.16-0.21x, H.264 decode about 2x behind). AI-assisted repo (CLAUDE.md, .claude/). The Opus numbers in the README belong to the separate Remade-With-Rust/rusty-opus fork of opus-rs, not to this repo.

notes: Numbers match the README and the crate READMEs; the record's figures are accurate, but the corrections separate per-core wins (MP3 decode, slight AAC) from thread-count wins (AAC, Vorbis), name which crate and which C encoder or decoder each belongs to, and add the MP3 control row that favours FFmpeg. The language already reads Rust; verify.py apply ignores the language key. If the catalog wants a component listing, rusty_mp3 (MP3 decode vs FFmpeg) is the only candidate with a per-core claim.
